qaraqara-charka-confederation.t: A confederation of Aymara-speaking peoples in the southern Bolivian highlands, renowned as warriors and later linked to the silver mines of Potosí.
qaraqara-charka-confederation.o: In the centuries after Tiwanaku's collapse, the Qaraqara and Charka formed a federation of peoples in the highlands of Potosí, Chuquisaca and northern Potosí in modern Bolivia, around 1200. The federation included groups such as the Chuy and Chicha.
qaraqara-charka-confederation.r: The confederation was organised in two halves led by the Qaraqara in the south and the Charka in the north, each under hereditary lords. It is known chiefly from a memorial written by its lords in 1582, which describes their service as soldiers for the Incas. The peoples herded llamas, farmed tubers and maize, and worked silver and other metals.
qaraqara-charka-confederation.e: The confederation came under Inca rule around 1460 and served the Incas in war. After the Spanish conquest, its lands formed the core of the Royal Audiencia of Charcas, and the silver mountain of Potosí, discovered in 1545, lay in Qaraqara territory.

qasim-khanate.t: A Tatar vassal state created by Moscow on the Oka, whose Muslim khans served the Russian rulers for over two centuries.
qasim-khanate.o: In 1452 Vasily II of Moscow granted the town of Gorodets Meshchersky on the Oka, later renamed Kasimov, to Qasim, a son of Ulugh Muhammad, founder of the Khanate of Kazan, who had entered Moscow's service. It became a small Tatar khanate under Moscow's protection.
qasim-khanate.r: Its khans, descendants of Genghis Khan, ruled a Tatar nobility and local Meshchera and Russian subjects, kept their Muslim faith and served in Moscow's armies. Moscow used them as rival candidates for the throne of Kazan, and Shah Ali of Kasimov was installed there more than once. The khan's mosque and the tomb of Shah Ali still stand in Kasimov.
qasim-khanate.e: The khanate gradually lost its independence, and its later rulers converted to Christianity or were controlled by Moscow. After the death of the last ruler, Fatima Sultan, in 1681, it was abolished and absorbed into the Tsardom of Russia.

que.t: Que, a Neo-Hittite kingdom of the Cilician plain around Adana, known for its horses and for bilingual inscriptions in Luwian and Phoenician.
que.o: After the Hittite collapse, a kingdom arose in the fertile Cilician plain, formerly Kizzuwatna. Its people called it Hiyawa, a name some link with the Greek Ahhiyawa, and its capital was Adana. Assyrian texts call it Que from the 9th century BCE.
que.r: Kings such as Awariku, the Urikki of Assyrian texts, ruled with Phoenician as a prestige language beside Luwian; bilingual inscriptions at Karatepe and Çineköy are key to deciphering Luwian hieroglyphs. Que bred horses, which the Bible says Solomon bought there.
que.e: Shalmaneser III of the Assyrian Empire campaigned against King Kate. Urikki became a vassal of Tiglath-Pileser III, and by 713 BCE Sargon II had made Que an Assyrian province.

qedarites.t: The most powerful Arab tribal confederation of the first millennium BCE, controlling desert routes from Syria to the oases of north Arabia.
qedarites.o: The Qedarites (biblical Kedar) appear in Assyrian records from the 8th century BCE as camel-herding Arabs of the Syrian desert and northern Arabia. Their centre was the oasis of Adummatu, modern Dumat al-Jandal, which held the shrine of their gods. Queen Zabibe paid tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III in 738 BCE, followed by Queen Samsi.
qedarites.r: They were led by kings and, unusually, by queens who also served as priestesses, among them Te'elhunu. The confederation controlled caravan routes carrying incense from south Arabia to the Levant and supplied camels and guides to imperial armies. Repeated revolts brought punitive campaigns: Sennacherib seized their idols, and Ashurbanipal fought Yauta son of Hazael in the 7th century BCE.
qedarites.e: Under the Achaemenid Empire the Qedarites kept their autonomy; Geshem the Arab, opponent of Nehemiah, and his son Qaynu, named king of Qedar on a silver bowl from Egypt, date to the 5th century BCE. By the 3rd century BCE their place was taken by the Nabataean Kingdom.

quadi.t: A Suebian people north of the middle Danube who, with the Marcomanni, fought Rome under Marcus Aurelius and later joined the great migration into Spain.
quadi.o: The Quadi settled in Moravia and western Slovakia, probably moving there from the Main region around the same time as the Marcomanni at the end of the 1st century BCE. They formed part of the realm of Maroboduus and later of the client kingdom of Vannius, established by Rome in 19.
quadi.r: Ruled by kings, often confirmed by Rome, the Quadi lived in villages, traded with Roman Pannonia and buried their elite with Roman imports. They joined the Marcomannic Wars from 166; the 'Rain Miracle' depicted on the Column of Marcus Aurelius took place on their territory. Rome built forward posts in their land such as Mušov.
quadi.e: In 374 the killing of their king Gabinius by a Roman officer provoked a raid into Pannonia, and Emperor Valentinian I died in 375 while confronting their envoys. In 406 many Quadi crossed the Rhine with the Vandals and Alans, probably becoming part of the Suebian kingdom in Spain.

qatna.t: Qatna, a wealthy Bronze Age kingdom near Homs whose intact royal tomb and palace show Syria's prosperity between Egypt, Mitanni and the Hittites.
qatna.o: Qatna, at Tell el-Mishrifeh, was refounded at the start of the 2nd millennium BCE inside huge square earthen ramparts. Its Amorite kings controlled central Syria and the caravan routes from the Euphrates to the coast, and became the main rivals of Yamhad.
qatna.r: In the Mari era King Ishhi-Addu allied with Shamshi-Adad and married his daughter to Yasmah-Addu. The royal palace held a hypogeum, found unplundered in 2002, with gold, ivory and the bones of generations of the royal family. Later kings left Akkadian archives with many Hurrian words.
qatna.e: In the 14th century BCE Qatna lay between the Mitanni Empire, the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom and the Hittite Empire. Its king Akizzi appealed to Egypt in the Amarna letters, but Hittite forces under Suppiluliuma I sacked the city c. 1340 BCE and it never recovered.

qarmatians-of-bahrain.t: A radical Isma'ili state in eastern Arabia, ruled by a council at al-Ahsa, that stole the Black Stone from Mecca in 930.
qarmatians-of-bahrain.o: In 899 the missionary Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi, preaching the coming of the Mahdi, won over Bedouin and peasants in eastern Arabia, then called Bahrain, and took al-Ahsa and Qatif. His state broke with the Fatimid Caliphate's claims to leadership and became a separate Qarmatian power.
qarmatians-of-bahrain.r: After Abu Sa'id, the state was governed by a council of his descendants and leading men. Visitors such as Nasir Khusraw reported that citizens paid no taxes, debts were interest free and thousands of African slaves worked the date groves. Under Abu Tahir the Qarmatians raided Basra and Kufa, attacked pilgrim caravans and in 930 sacked Mecca, carrying the Black Stone to al-Ahsa until 951.
qarmatians-of-bahrain.e: Their power declined after defeats by the Fatimids and the Buyids and the loss of Oman. In 1077 Abd Allah al-Uyuni, a local chief, overthrew them with help from the Seljuk Empire and founded the Uyunid Emirate.

quitu-cara.t: The peoples of the Quito basin before the Incas, remembered in Ecuadorian tradition as the Kingdom of Quito ruled by the Shyris, a story many historians doubt.
quitu-cara.o: The Quitu were the inhabitants of the highland basin where Quito now stands, settled since at least the first millennium CE. In 1789 the Jesuit historian Juan de Velasco wrote that the Cara people came from the coast around 980 and founded a kingdom ruled by kings called Shyris, which united the northern highlands.
quitu-cara.r: Archaeology shows a landscape of local chiefdoms around Quito and its valleys, with farming of maize and potatoes and markets where goods from the coast and Amazon were traded. Velasco's account of a centralised kingdom with a line of Shyri kings has no support from earlier chronicles and is widely regarded as legend, though it became a cornerstone of Ecuadorian national identity.
quitu-cara.e: The Quito region fell to the Incas in the late 15th century and became their northern capital under Huayna Capac. After Atahualpa's capture, the Inca general Rumiñahui held Quito until the Spanish took it in 1534.
